title: Why do the example first
idea: Deciding the expected output before coding saves you from guessing later. The example is your target to aim at.

exercises.prompt: If you code first and never decide what output you want, what goes wrong?
options: You can't tell if the result is right or wrong
exercises.explanation: With no target, any output looks as good as any other. The example gives you something to compare against.

exercises.prompt: Having an expected output lets you spot a mistake quickly.
exercises.explanation: If the screen shows something different from your example, you instantly know something's off.

exercises.prompt: Task: show 'Welcome'. You expect the output to be Welcome. The program shows 'welcom'. What does the example tell you?
options: The output is wrong — it doesn't match
exercises.explanation: Your example said Welcome. The screen said welcom. They don't match, so the code is wrong. The example caught it.

exercises.prompt: A worked example is only useful if it exactly describes the output you want.
exercises.explanation: A vague example ('something like Welcome') can't catch a small mistake. Be exact.

exercises.prompt: Put the smart order in place.
blocks: Compare the real output to the example
exercises.explanation: Example first, then code, then compare. The example comes before the code so it can judge it.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: 'I'll just know if it looks right.' Why is that risky?
options: A small error is easy to miss without an exact target
exercises.explanation: The human eye misses small slips. An exact written example makes mismatches obvious.

exercises.prompt: Which are true about an expected-output example? (pick all)
options: It describes exactly what should appear
It is a target to compare against
It changes every time you look at it
exercises.explanation: Decided first, exact, and a stable target. It does NOT change each time — a moving target is useless.

exercises.prompt: Working the example first is part of understanding the task.
exercises.explanation: To write the right output, you must truly understand what the task asks. The example proves you get it.

exercises.prompt: Task: show the number 7. What is the exact expected output?
exercises.explanation: Just the digit 7 appears. Our example is precise: 7, nothing else.

exercises.prompt: The best time to write your example is...
exercises.explanation: Before coding. Then the code has a clear goal, and you have a ready-made check.
